title: I built a Cold War naval Battleship game with an AI as the coder, playable demo in the browse
author: Fincut

comments.author: Fincut
comments.body:
**Setup and workflow, technical version.** Game: Bearing Unknown, Three.js, the whole client is one HTML file built by a Python script. Repo on GitHub, 216 numbered versions since May. I run the project side, the AI (Claude, through the desktop app linked to my Windows laptop) writes all code.

**Two machines, clearly separated.**

**1. My laptop (Windows, RTX 3080).** The repo lives here. The AI has the project folder linked and edits files in place, no copy and paste through chat. It also gets a sandboxed Linux shell on my machine with only that folder mounted, so it can grep, patch, run the Python build, ffmpeg and node directly on my files. Deleting is blocked in that sandbox by design; it moves things into a _to_delete folder and I empty it. Anything that needs my hardware (Edge with the real GPU, the installer build, git push) I run myself as a copy-ready PowerShell one-liner the AI posts, always one step with a "done when" criterion.

**2. The AI's own Linux container in the cloud.** Headless Chromium with SwiftShader, Python with PIL and numpy, ffmpeg, Playwright. It uses this for everything that does not need a GPU: serving a copy of the demo on a local port, taking screenshots at phone and desktop sizes, measuring images numerically (black level, saturation, pixel diffs) instead of eyeballing them, trying code before it touches my repo.

**GPU work goes through job files.** The AI wrote a capture tool (Node and Playwright) that launches Edge on my laptop with the GPU, loads the built game, forces graphics settings via localStorage, drives the game through an injected JS hook (place fleets, start the battle, fire a salvo), and for film steps the game loop by hand at a fixed 30 fps so the output is smooth regardless of render time. I run it with a JSON job per scene; it writes stills and frame sequences into the repo; the AI reads them back, measures them, cuts the website loop with ffmpeg. Today that pipeline found its own bug: a muzzle flash overlay stayed frozen because the tool had stopped requestAnimationFrame for everything, not just the game loop. Every capture had a grey veil, the game never did. Fixed by queuing the other callbacks and flushing them per manual tick.

**Balancing:** a headless simulator, AI vs AI, about 5.5 million games, tuned until both fleets won equally often whoever starts.

**Backend:** plain PHP on shared hosting. Anonymous analytics (no IPs, no cookies), and a double opt-in mailing list where addresses are stored encrypted with a key only I hold.

**Continuity:** the AI loses context on long sessions, so the repo carries an architecture document and a changelog with one entry per version, plus the standing rules (one step at a time, no prototypes, no silent deviations, every commit is a version plus a build). New session, read those first, continue.

**Releases:** Python build for the web demo, uploaded by FTP; same source packaged as a Windows build for Steam.

**Free demo, no download:** https://wildstone-studios.com/?k=aigamedev
